data.title: The 6 races that could decide Senate control
data.description:
The midterm tug-of-war for Senate control will come down to half a dozen coin-toss contests, giving both parties a path to the upper chamber majority. 

All six seats rated as “toss-ups” by DDHQ — Texas, Maine, Alaska, Ohio, Iowa and Kansas — are currently held by Republicans. The GOP’s best chance of flipping a seat is in Michigan, where DDHQ gives Democrats a 73 percent chance of winning. 

As of the Friday before Election Day, DDHQ’s forecasts showed Democrats with the advantage in both chambers — though their chances were more uncertain in the Senate, with a 60 percent chance of a flip, than in the House, where they had an 82 percent chance. 

Here’s what to know about the races that will decide Senate control: 

Texas

The Senate race in Texas has been one of this cycle’s most closely watched, from Democrat James Talarico’s rising-star bid amid GOP-friendly redistricting to incumbent Sen. John Cornyn’s (R) dramatic loss to Attorney General Ken Paxton in a tough Republican primary runoff. 

It’s become one of the most expensive non-presidential contests in U.S. history, pulling in more than half a billion dollars in what both sides frame as an existential fight for the Lone Star State’s political future. 

Texas Democrats haven’t won a statewide race in decades, but they’re hopeful that Talarico’s unity-focused, faith-driven bid can compete with Paxton’s controversy-laden, MAGA-faithful campaign amid frustration with the White House. 

Mere days before the election, Talarico was leading Paxton by just under four points in polling averages from DDHQ, with a 60 percent probability of flipping the seat. A recent Emerson College Poll found the race in a dead heat and noted that Libertarian candidate Ted Brown could pull some support on Election Day, potentially tipping the race in Talarico’s favor.

Hispanic and Latino voters could also be a game-changer. The bloc, which makes up roughly a third of the Texas electorate, moved toward President Trump in 2024, but appears to be returning to the left this cycle, frustrated by the president’s handling of the economy and immigration. 

Iowa

One of Democrats’ toughest flip opportunities will be in Iowa, where Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson hopes to hold back Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek in the race to replace retiring Sen. Joni Ernst (R).

According to DDHQ’s Friday forecasts, Hinson was headed into Election Day with a 55 percent chance of holding onto her seat as she led Turek by a single point in polling averages. 

“Both Democrats and Republicans privately believe that if only one GOP candidate in our Toss Up states hangs on, it will be Iowa,” Cook Political Report’s Jessica Taylor wrote in an analysis ahead of the election, noting that Hinson has “deftly distanced herself” from some of Trump’s unpopular policies. 

But Trump is still “deeply underwater” in Iowa, Taylor said, and Democrat Rob Sand’s gubernatorial bid could also be key to helping turnout for Turek. 

“Ultimately, Democrats are poised to capitalize on Trump’s tumbling image and discouraged base. The true test may be whether even the best GOP candidates of the cycle — in Maine and Iowa — can survive a looming blue wave.” 

Ohio

Former Sen. Sherrod Brown’s (D) comeback bid in Ohio could restore Democrats to the Buckeye State’s Senate delegation just two years after he lost to Sen. Bernie Moreno (R).

Brown is challenging incumbent Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed to fill Vice President Vance’s Senate vacancy, in the special election to fill out the rest of Vance’s term, which runs through 2028. 

Alongside Texas, it’s become one of the priciest-ever Senate races. Brown brought in $23.1 million to Husted’s $5 million in the third quarter alone, but GOP-aligned groups have surged more than $100 million into the state to attack Brown. 

Husted has Trump’s support — including comments on his physique that have gone viral in the closing days of the race — but Brown boasts higher name recognition and rare success as a Democrat in the red-leaning state. 

As of Friday afternoon, Brown had a 55 percent probability of flipping the seat as he led Husted by roughly 3 points in DDHQ’s polling averages, according to The Hill’s partner. 

“After Texas, Ohio is the next most vulnerable GOP-held seat on our list,” Taylor wrote for Cook Political Report, pointing out that Husted has probably been hurt by Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s troubled campaign for Ohio governor.

Maine

Sen. Susan Collins (R) is aiming for a sixth term as a rare Republican to win in blue-leaning Maine. She’s been bolstered by her political legacy and name-ID as Democrats dealt with a tumultuous primary season.

But her challenger, Democrat Troy Jackson, is still favored to beat her. The former state Senate president, who unsuccessfully ran for governor this cycle, replaced progressive oyster farmer Graham Platner on the ticket when Platner’s bid imploded amid sexual misconduct allegations.

In a state that went to Vice President Harris in the 2024 presidential election, Collins is leaning on her seniority and stressing her distance from Trump — particularly on tariffs, which have strained Mainers’ pocketbooks and caused problems with Canada, a vital trading partner that shares a 600-mile border with the Pine Tree State.

But though she’s long enjoyed comfortable reelection numbers, she won by a narrower 9 points in 2020 after her controversial vote to confirm Justice Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court, which has continued to dog her in 2026. 

Jackson had climbed to a 60 percent chance of ousting Collins in DDHQ’s Friday forecast, leading the incumbent by roughly 3 points in polling averages. 

Kansas

Kansas hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in nearly a century, so its “toss-up” rating tees up what could be one of the cycle’s biggest surprises.  

Democrat Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor and former Republican, has put Sen. Roger Marshall (R), an OB-GYN backed by Trump, on defense in the red stronghold. 

In DDHQ’s Friday forecast, Marshall had dropped to a 53 percent chance of holding the seat for the GOP, as Hamilton climbed to a polling-average lead of nearly three points. 

As of Friday, Democrats had spent $16 million more on the race than Republicans, according to data tracked by AdImpact. 

Experts see the latest numbers out of Kansas as a clear sign of Democratic momentum across the country in this year’s midterms. 

“A Democrat winning Kansas, even if that candidate is leading the polls, has got to be considered an upset,” said Decision Desk HQ’s chief elections analyst Geoffrey Skelley. 

“If Democrats win Kansas, not only is it winning a state that they haven’t won in a Senate race since 1932, the longest such drought in the country for either major party, but … for the Senate control question, it gives Democrats sort of an additional card to play,” he said. “If they were to win Kansas, maybe they don’t need to flip Iowa. Maybe you know, maybe Alaska, you know, is less of a concern now.” 

Alaska

Alaska offers Democrats another serious pickup opportunity in what should have been a longshot based on recent trends. 

Democrat Mary Peltola, who lost Alaska’s at-large House seat in 2024, is running on a “fish, family, freedom” platform as Sullivan touts his Trump alignment in the red state. 

Peltola had a 60 percent shot of taking the seat in DDHQ’s Friday forecast, and was ahead by less than two points in the polling average. 

But neither candidate was polling past 50 percent, opening up the possibility that the race kicks into a second round of ranked-choice tabulations. Maine is the only other state with ranked-choice voting statewide. Alaska’s sprawling map with isolated communities lets ballots be counted up to 15 days after the election, provided they were postmarked in time — which could prolong the suspense after polls close on Tuesday. 

The race was also rocked in its home stretch by controversy over a candidate with the same name as the incumbent. 

The Trump administration filed a lawsuit in late October seeking to block certification of the Senate election if the incumbent loses with Daniel J. Sullivan, who goes by Dan Sullivan, also on the ballot. Peltola’s campaign and national Democrats denied New York Times reporting this week that they coordinated to recruit candidates who could pull support from the sitting senator.

data.title: Will Tuesday be a a blue wave or just an anti-Trump surge?
data.description:
Poll after poll shows the Democrats comfortably retaking the House come Nov. 3, with a number also giving them a slightly better than even chance of taking the Senate. Maybe. But I’ve been around this business a long time, and something feels a bit less “bluey” by the day.       

To be sure, the Republican brand is in a world of hurt right now, with tens of millions of voters not willing to let the party wiggle off the hook of accountability, since Republicans control the White House, the Senate and the House. Blaming the Biden administration may work with much of the MAGA base, but it frays into incredulity for the rest of the voting blocs when they stop to realize that the Trump administration has been in power for coming up on two years.          

Not surprisingly to anyone paying the remotest bit of attention over the last decade, in one way or another, all partisan roads seem to lead back to President Trump. Somewhat ironically for this election cycle, should the Republicans lose across the board, it was Trump himself who blazed one of those rhetorically poisonous roads back to him and his party by repeatedly telling Americans, “Vote as if I am on the ballot.”  

Watch what you wish for.  

To be sure, millions of Americans in and out of the MAGA base still strongly believe in the president, his brand and his policies. Many believe he saved our nation. But viewing the flip side of that coin, some could certainly make the case that a large percentage of the votes Joe Biden got in 2020 and Kamala Harris got in 2024 were not votes for those two Democratic presidential nominees so much as votes against Trump. If one buys into that theory, then it’s also reasonable to believe that the “I only voted because I want Trump gone” demographic is still out there — and may have grown in the last few years. Such voters are eager to accept Trump’s challenge. 

Many Republicans I speak with believe that their party is bleeding votes, from independents, youths. minorities, even faith-based votes. And the main reason for the vote bleed is absolutely no mystery. The administration can sing the praises of a rising stock market and growing 401(k)s until they are blue in the face. These positives mean little or nothing to voters whose paychecks are shrinking by the month as they cope with higher gasoline and grocery prices, home ownership increasingly out of reach, and a widening disappointment regarding the war with Iran. 

The pendulum that determines national elections regularly is pushed to that cycle’s winning side by just slivers of the vote in certain districts, counties and states. At the moment, that pendulum is swinging back to the left, even despite a veritable laundry list of accomplishments authored by this president and his administration over the course of the last two years: historically lower crime rates; a closed and protected border; increased energy dominance; and the creation of almost 70 million Trump Accounts for kids.   

Even so, many Trump supporters and Republicans still refuse to believe that a blue wave is about to swamp their president and party.  They honestly wonder how they could be losing to nothing but sheer hatred of Donald Trump. While the Democratic leadership understandably pounces on the “affordability” issue at every opportunity, their own answers to that “crisis” are either paper-thin or nonexistent.   

And yet, the polls continue to favor them. 

Is that enough for the Democrats to have a great day on Nov. 3, even with no real solutions to the issues plaguing this nation? We’ll just have to wait and see.

Douglas MacKinnon is a former White House and Pentagon official.

data.title: Iran's Supreme Leader threatens US with response if strikes are launched after midterms
data.description:
Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei issued a stark message on Friday, warning the U.S. against its reported plans to resume strikes against the country following the midterm elections. 

Khamenei directed senior Iranian military officials in a meeting to deliver an “immediate, impactful response without geographical limitations,” according to Iran’s official IRNA news agency. 

The leader reportedly instructed these military leaders to update their target database “to ensure that all physical and non-physical assets” of the U.S. and Israeli armies are brought within reach of the Iranian armed forces.  

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment. 

On Friday, several outlets reported that the U.S. had notified several Arab countries to prepare for a short U.S. military campaign following the Nov. 3 elections, with fresh attacks expected as soon as the following day, three senior Gulf Arab officials told MS NOW.  

President Trump promised earlier this month he would not launch strikes against Iran ahead of the midterms, as he continues to face pressure to wind down this war amid rising energy prices and other costs tied to the conflict. 

The war, which began with joint U.S.-Israeli strikes launched on Feb. 28, has now stretched over eight months. The conflict has cost the U.S. around $47 billion, according to an Oct. 16 estimate from U.S. Central Command. 

At a rally last week, the president indicated his administration “may do another little Epic Fury” if Iran refuses to meet U.S. demands, in reference to the U.S.’s military operations against Tehran, dubbed “Operation Epic Fury.”

“If they’re smart, they’ll just say, ‘Let’s get down to business,’” the president said. “But, you know, I doubt they’ll do that because perhaps they’re not smart.”

The Trump administration has also waged a massive effort to isolate Iran’s economy, called “Operation Economic Outcast,” by placing sanctions on Iranian oil and imposing a U.S. naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz, a key oil trading corridor. 

The Treasury Department said in a Friday report that the campaign was “decimating” Iran’s economy, finding headline inflation in the country reached 90 percent in September.

data.title: DC, Virginia sue to block Trump's triumphal arch
data.description:
Washington, D.C., and Virginia sued the National Parks Service and Interior Department to block President Trump’s proposed triumphal arch on Saturday, a new court filing shows.

The planned arch would resemble arches in other cities, including Paris’s Arc de Triomphe, and be constructed on the border between D.C. and Virginia.

In the court filing, the plaintiffs call the arch “flagrantly unlawful” because Trump did not seek congressional authorization to construct the project.

“In their rush to break ground on the Arch, Defendants have made only half-hearted gestures at complying with these requirements,” the lawsuit reads. “Perhaps recognizing that the project is legally indefensible, Defendants have made clear that they will attempt to outrun judicial review.”

The president has pushed forward with his efforts to renovate Washington despite frequent lawsuits and a lack of congressional authorization. One particular case involved the White House ballroom, in which the East Wing was demolished and construction on the ballroom began immediately.

When sued over the project, the Supreme Court ruled in the Trump administration’s favor after Trump argued the ballroom construction needed to continue for national security purposes.

The plaintiffs in Saturday’s lawsuit say they hope to avoid a similar situation with the arch.

“It is entirely foreseeable that, once construction begins, Defendants will argue—as they have done in other cases—that an order halting construction would irreparably harm the federal government, pose security risks, and impermissibly alter the status quo they have unilaterally created,” the lawsuit reads.

In a statement to The Hill, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones called the project “an affront” to Arlington National Cemetery, where the arch would be located.

“President Trump’s illegal vanity project is an affront to this hallowed ground and the extraordinary sacrifices it represents,” Jones said. “The Commonwealth has a solemn duty and a profound interest in preserving the dignity of this sacred place.”

The Parks Service did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

The proposals for the arch at one point included military plans, as Trump said it would be used for snipers and drones, though the final plans submitted to the city did not include the military complex.

Arlington County, Va. previously sued the Trump administration to block the arch in early October.

data.title: Federal appeals court lifts Idaho ruling permitting abortions for women's health
data.description:
A federal appeals court paused a judge’s earlier ruling that ordered Idaho to allow exceptions to its abortion ban in cases where a doctor deemed it necessary to protect the mother’s health. 

In a 2-1 decision issued on Friday, the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals found that a doctor who sued over the state’s ban was unlikely to prevail on claims that the right to a health-saving abortion is constitutional. 

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in its 2022 Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization decision there was no constitutional right to abortion, overturning its landmark 1973 Roe v. Wade decision. 

Idaho and a dozen other states issued near-total abortion bans following the high court’s ruling. Abortion is restricted in an additional nine states, according to the Center for Reproductive Rights. 

The appeals court’s pause applies to an 81-page decision issued by U.S. District Judge Lynn Winmill in August, which the federal judge later limited to bar the state law’s enforcement against the plaintiff, Stacey Seyb.

“We think it unlikely that Dr. Seyb will be able to square the district court’s perspective on the history and tradition concerning abortions with the Supreme Court’s perspective in Dobbs,” the appeals court said in its decision. 

Circuit Judges Kim Wardlaw and Consuelo Callahan made up the court’s majority in this ruling. Wardlaw, a Clinton appointee, issued a concurring opinion, in which she noted that the appeals court was “bound by the decisions of the Supreme Court.”

“As such, in light of the Dobbs majority opinion, I join Judge Callahan in concluding that Defendants have shown a likelihood of success on the merits,” Wardlaw continued. 

In a dissenting opinion, Circuit Judge Marsha Berzon found the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision applied only to elective abortions and warned that some women could be “required to continue their pregnancies at serious, permanent risk to their health” because of this ruling. 

“The risk, absent the injunction, to Dr. Seyb’s pregnant patients of serious and lasting harm short of death is definitionally a risk of irreparable injury,” she wrote.

data.title: Ricketts leads independent candidate Osborn by 6 points in latest Nebraska Senate poll
data.description:
Just ahead of Election Day, Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.) leads his independent challenger Dan Osborn, a new survey of the Nebraska Senate race shows.

The New York Times/Siena University poll shows Ricketts leading Osborn by 6 points, 49 percent to 43 percent, respectively, among likely Nebraska voters.

November’s election is the second cycle in a row in which no Democrat was on the Nebraska Senate ballot. In 2024 and 2026, Democrats backed Osborn instead of supporting their own candidate, hoping to have a better shot at defeating the GOP.

While Osborn has not said he would caucus with one party or the other in the U.S. Senate, most Nebraska voters see him as more aligned with Democrats, the Times poll shows. Fifty-five percent think Osborn is more similar to Democrats, while just 33 percent believe he is more of an independent. Only 4 percent said he was more of a Republican. 

Being branded as a Democrat does not get you far in Nebraska, where 71 percent of voters said they were dissatisfied with the Democratic Party.

Still, Osborn is running just 6 points behind in a state President Trump carried by more than 20 points in 2024. The president’s approval is underwater in the Times poll, but just barely — 47 percent approve and 49 percent disapprove of his job performance.

Osborn came within just over 6 points from winning in 2024 as well, when he ran a surprisingly competitive race against Sen. Deb Fischer (R).

Since that campaign however, Republicans have had more time to define Osborn and paint him as a Democrat, which may have hurt his image with voters.

Democrats in South Dakota and Idaho also have no candidate on the ballot and are backing independent challengers to GOP Sens. Mike Rounds and Jim Risch, respectively. Montana Democrats attempted to do the same, backing independent Seth Bodnar against Republican Kurt Alme, but Democrat Alani Bankhead, who won her party’s primary, refused to drop out of the race.

While Ricketts leads in the Senate race, Democrats in Nebraska’s House races are running surprisingly strong. The party is heavily favored to flip the open 2nd Congressional District, and is even contesting the 1st district, represented by Rep. Mike Flood (R), which Trump won by double digits in 2024.

Trump traveled to Nebraska to rally for Ricketts in early October, one of his many stops in deep-red states that his party is struggling to hold in the midterms.

The Times/Siena poll was conducted from Oct. 23 to 29 among 809 likely Nebraska voters. The poll has a margin of error of +/- 4.2 points.

data.title: Alaska's decoy scandal brings back the usual suspects for shady election tactics
data.description:
Marc Elias is back. The notorious Democratic lawyer who played a critical role in the 2016 Russia hoax is again in the news. His law firm has been identified by the New York Times as part of the expanding scandal involving Democratic effort to confuse voters in Alaska with a decoy candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan.

For those familiar with Elias’s checkered history, this is a case of rounding up the usual suspects.

The scandal involving Democratic candidate Mary Peltola has quickly snowballed this week. A New York Times blockbuster investigative report quotes former staff who claim she knew of a cynical effort by her own campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to confuse voters by recruiting and fielding a decoy “Dan Sullivan” candidate in the race against incumbent Sen. Daniel S. Sullivan (R-Alaska). State and federal investigations are now unfolding, with dozens of federal subpoenas raining down on Alaska.

The effort to get voters to cast mistaken ballots is grossly unethical and, even in these rage-filled times, a uniquely disgraceful scheme. Peltola and the Democratic Party had long denied any involvement in the other Sullivan’s candidacy. So when the Times produced evidence that she allegedly knew, and that Democratic staffers and lawyers had been deeply involved from the beginning, many of us were surprised — that is, until the name “Marc Elias” emerged. Then it made more sense.

The Elias Law Group was already in the news this election cycle for threatening reporters with defamation lawsuits if they kept asking questions about the health of former Gov. Roy Cooper, the Democratic nominee for Senate in North Carolina. Earlier, Elias caused a stir during an unsuccessful Democratic gerrymandering effort, raising the idea that Democratic leaders could abolish the entire Virginia government after courts blocked their attempted radical redistricting plan.

The fact that figures such as Peltola and Cooper wanted to be associated with any law firm headed by Elias is itself an indictment of their judgment and standards.

Despite his losses in cases such as National Republican Senatorial Committee v. Federal Election Commission, Elias is still a favorite of many on the left thanks to his aggression and partisan fervor. The controversies that make him notorious to many make him popular with others.

Elias was the general counsel to the Clinton presidential campaign when it secretly funded the infamous Steele Dossier and pushed the false Alfa Bank conspiracy theory. (His fellow Perkins Coie partner, Michael Sussmann, was later indicted but acquitted for making a false statement to the FBI.)

Clinton campaign officials lied to reporters during the 2016 campaign, denying any involvement in the Steele Dossier. Journalists discovered the truth after the election — that the Clinton campaign had hidden payments for the dossier as “legal fees” among the $5.6 million paid to Perkins Coie. New York Times reporter Ken Vogel said that when tried to report the story, Elias “pushed back vigorously, saying ‘You (or your sources) are wrong.’”

Times reporter Maggie Haberman later observed that “Folks involved in funding this lied about it, and with sanctimony, for a year.” The Federal Election Commission ultimately sanctioned the Clinton campaign for the subterfuge.

While raising money as the self-proclaimed defenders of democracy, Elias’s group has been involved in gerrymandering and efforts criticized as seeking to invalidate Republican votes, including unsuccessful efforts to challenge Democratic electoral losses.

In Maryland, Elias’s team supported another abusive gerrymandering scheme that a court found not only violated Maryland law but the state constitution’s equal protection, free speech and free elections clauses. The court found that the proposed map “subverts the will of those governed.”

One media site accused Elias and his group of “making millions off gerrymandering efforts” while publicly denouncing Republican gerrymandering.

In 2024, Elias’s legal team was also accused of pushing “to bar third-party presidential candidates — including Cornel West — from swing state ballots where they might siphon votes” from Democratic nominee Kamala Harris.

Likewise, the New York Times reported that the Elias firm’s work “on behalf of a Soros-funded PAC in Texas … was opposed by a left-leaning election watchdog as undermining laws intended to limit the influence of major donors.”

His group’s work for New York’s redistricting effort was ridiculed as not only ignoring the express will of the voters and also effectively negating Republicans’ votes.

In 2024, the Chief Judge of the Western District of Wisconsin criticized the Elias Law Group for one of its challenges. Judge James Peterson (an Obama appointee) said that the argument “simply does not make any sense.”

Now, Elias’s group is linked to the decoy scandal in Alaska, which allegedly aimed to make voters cast mistaken ballots. What distinguishes lawyers involved in this type of voter disruption is less their talent as their willingness. There are simply some things that most lawyers will not do.

There is also a difference in how lawyers are treated in such controversies. It often seems that in election controversies involving Republican lawyers are more likely to end with bar charges and disbarments. Take John Eastman, the former Trump lawyer disbarred in California after a state bar panel found that he had pushed unfounded legal theories and conspired to obstruct the electoral vote count on Jan. 6, 2021.

Although I publicly disagreed with Eastman’s theories, I opposed the effort to disbar him as setting a dangerous precedent for lawyers seeking to advance novel or unpopular theories of recovery or liability. After all, lawyers on the left routinely advance dubious theories, including some that are more ideologically than legally driven. Such controversies rarely rise to the level of disbarment, especially when more appropriate sanctions are available, ranging from reprimands to fines.

Eastman is currently asking the Supreme Court to overturn his disbarment. It is unlikely that Elias Law Group or Peltola’s lawyers will face similar disbarment efforts — nor should they, in my view, unless they were involved in criminal conduct. But the disparate treatment afforded to counsel in this country by party remains a growing concern. What draws a shower of bar complaints for Republican lawyers brings a windfall of clients for Democratic lawyers.

The New York Times has produced sources alleging that lawyers for Peltola’s campaign were involved in this effort, even though they previously told a federal court that they “lack knowledge or information” and “deny any allegation about those purposes.” Such filings and statements could raise ethical or even criminal questions in investigations at both the state and federal levels.

Meanwhile, though, tens of thousands of voters in Alaska have already cast ballots that included the decoy Sullivan candidate. This could result in a nasty fight in Congress if Peltola prevails in the vote count. And when it happens, that is where we will find Marc Elias in his element.

Jonathan Turley is a law professor and the New York Times best-selling author of “Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution.”

data.title: Trump administration attempts to bypass restrictions on sending Afghan refugees to Afghanistan: Reports
data.description:
The Trump administration is proceeding with plans to effectively deport some Afghan refugees to Afghanistan, despite concerns they could become targets of the Taliban there, according to several reports.

Dozens of Afghan immigrants have been detained in Louisiana and over 150 people are expected to be deported, making this among the largest single deportations of Afghans, according to The New York Times.  

The U.S. is restricted from sending refugees straight to Afghanistan, as the country lacks diplomatic relations with the Taliban. Instead, the Trump administration plans to send the group to Pakistan, where they are widely expected to be sent to Afghanistan.

The Hill has reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment.

Bloomberg was the first to report on the initial details of this plan earlier this week, citing a government official with knowledge of the plans. 

The deportation flight to Pakistan could depart as soon as Monday morning, according to NBC News. 

In the past, the U.S. has deported some Afghans to Afghanistan through intermediary countries, but these cases have involved immigrants with terrorism or other serious criminal charges. 

This is the latest in the Trump administration’s efforts to carry out a widespread deportation campaign across the country. 

President Trump blocked the admission of Afghans and other refugees, and his administration has deported thousands of people to countries where they have no ties. The Supreme Court is set to rule on the legality of these third-country deportations this term.  

Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), the ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, slammed this latest deportation plan in a statement shared to social media on Friday. 

“It is reprehensible that the Trump Administration plans to deport hundreds of Afghans, including women, children and those who supported U.S. forces, to Pakistan – who then risk being sent back into the hands of the Taliban. Congress must stand against this,” Shaheen said. 

Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), who sits on the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, similarly criticized the move. 

“We made a promise to our Afghan allies—that after aiding & protecting our troops during the conflict in Afghanistan, America would not abandon them,” he wrote in a social media post. “This Administration is betraying that promise, deporting them to potential torture & death.”

data.title: Live updates: Trump telerallies planned in 19 states; Atlanta G20 meeting continues after early tensions
data.description:
President Trump is slated to speak at telerallies across the country Saturday, marking his last scheduled campaign appearance in several key battlegrounds before Election Day next week.

Trump is set to appear in virtual events in at least 19 states — Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Colorado, Florida, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Mexico, New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Texas and Virginia. The rallies will run at 4 p.m., 4:30 p.m. and 5 p.m. EDT.

The Republican National Committee first announced these telerallies Thursday after Trump canceled two in-person appearances in Kansas and Iowa — a move he walked back the next day. The president said during a Friday night rally in Daytona Beach, Fla., individuals from the two states called him and said, “We just want to make sure that we win.”

“I thought this was it. I thought I could relax. 28 days in a row of this crap is a lot. It’s a lot. My voice is about operating at about 49.2 percent,” Trump said Friday. “And then they called me in Iowa, and they called me in Kansas, and they said, ‘Sir, would it be possible to do a little rally of about 50,000 people each?'”

Meanwhile, Group of 20 diplomats will convene in Atlanta for the second day of its annual Foreign Ministers’ meeting. The gathering got heated on its first day, with its U.S. hosts deciding not to carry out the “family photo” tradition after several members refused to appear in a picture alongside a Russian official due to his country’s war in Ukraine.

Follow live below.

data.title: What a diploma measures when A's are the new normal
data.description:
Early decision applications are going out this fall, most of them due by mid-November, and the families sending them are committing to a very large bill. What they receive at the end of four years is a transcript and a diploma, and it is fair to ask what those two documents now report. 

Two issues answer the question, and they run in opposite directions. 

The first is grades. Stuart Rojstaczer and Christopher Healy collected grading records from American colleges and universities going back to 1940. In 1960, they found, C was the most common grade in the country, and D’s and F’s together outnumbered A’s. In their latest data, from the late 2000s, the A was the most common grade, at about 43 percent of all letter grades. That is 28 percentage points higher than in 1960, which means the A had nearly tripled its share. 

The most selective schools have gone furthest. By Harvard’s own count, A’s made up 24 percent of all grades awarded in 2005, 40 percent in 2015 and 60 percent in 2025.

Princeton tried to hold the line. In 2004 it told every department to hold A-range grades to less than 35 percent. Ten years later its faculty voted the limit away, after years of student complaints that it hurt them against applicants from schools with no such limit. Princeton’s own review found no measurable harm, but the perception was enough. Once most schools inflate, a school that grades honestly looks as though it is penalizing its own graduates, and few institutions will bear that cost for long.

Harvard is about to test that: In May, its faculty voted 458 to 201 to limit A’s to 20 percent of each course’s enrollment plus four students, starting in the fall of 2027. 

The second issue is effort, and it fell. Philip Babcock and Mindy Marks assembled half a century of time-use surveys. Full-time students in 1961 put about 40 hours a week into class and studying. By 2003, the figure was about 27 hours. The authors found the decline broad-based and not easily explained by students working more, choosing different majors or changes in who was enrolling. Over the same decades in which the A nearly tripled, the work behind it fell by about a third. 

Direct tests of learning cover a shorter span but point the same way. Richard Arum and Josipa Roksa followed students at more than two dozen four-year colleges as they took the Collegiate Learning Assessment in 2005, 2007 and 2009. After four years, 36 percent showed no significant improvement.

That is one cohort in one decade, not a 50-year trend. Still, it is the wrong result for anyone who would defend the grading record by arguing that students simply got better. If the A of 2008 stood for more learning than the A of 1960, students should have been working more and testing better. They were working less, and more than a third finished college testing about where they started. 

The consequences reach well beyond campus, because a grade is a piece of information, and so is a degree. Bryan Caplan and other economists who study signaling argue that much of a degree’s value comes from what it tells an employer about the holder: that he is reasonably able, conscientious and willing to finish what he starts.

Such a signal is worth something only while it is scarce. When few people held degrees and few grades were A’s, both told an employer something. When nearly everyone can send the signal, it stops sorting anyone, and what the employer is left reading is noise. 

Employers respond the way any buyer of information would. They ask for a bachelor’s degree for jobs most current holders do without one, and they lean on other proxies, such as the prestige of the school or a personal connection. Each student who buys the credential is acting sensibly for himself, but taken together, the whole population pays more for a signal that tells less, and no one ends up ahead. 

None of this calls for a federal grading standard or a mandated curriculum. The four-year degree bundles at least three different things. One is real skill, which could be delivered by shorter, rigorous programs in specific fields. Another is the signal, which could be supplied by portable certifications that employers assess for themselves. The third is a few years of growing up, which apprenticeships, service and work can also provide. 

The bundle survives because most of the federal student aid is attached to it, and the institutions selling it have every incentive to keep the pieces together. Take away the subsidy that props up the bundle, let the pieces compete on their own, and the diploma will have to start measuring something again or else lose its customers. 

Families writing checks this fall are paying dearly for a transcript on which the top grade has become the ordinary one. They deserve to know what they are buying. 

Jeffrey Janik is the author of “University for All: A Societal Disaster.”
